newsitem.title: MEXICO: US gave Mexico list of drug suspects but no proof.
newsitem.headline: US gave Mexico list of drug suspects but no proof.

text.p: The United States gave President Ernesto Zedillo's team a list of top Mexican officials suspected of drug ties but the information was not acted upon because no proof was supplied, a well-placed Mexican government source told Reuters.

The source, speaking on condition he not be identified, confirmed late on Tuesday that a member of Zedillo's team had received the list of names from U.S. officials in the run-up to the Dec. 1, 1994 start of the Zedillo administration.

"We told them (the Americans) we needed proof if this list was to be useful for us," the Mexican source said. "No proof was ever supplied ... Later on, the Americans themselves told us not to take that list too seriously."

The New York Times reported on Sunday that two state governors' names were on the list of "about 15 current and former Mexican officials", which it said was handed to Zedillo's team by U.S. ambassador to Mexico James Jones.

Both the governors, Sonora leader Manlio Fabio Beltrones and Morelos ruler Jorge Carrillo Olea, have strongly denied any link to drug traffickers. Local analysts noted that Mexican media have accused Beltrones in the past of drug links, something the governor has always rejected.
The U.S. embassy in Mexico has refused to confirm or deny the existence of a list of drug suspects or its delivery to Mexican officials.

But Robert Gelbard, the assistant U.S. secretary of state for narcotics matters, told a congressional panel in Washington on Tuesday that "we have raised concerns about individuals with the government of Mexico over time."
"There are individuals about whom we have been very concerned, deeply concerned. And we have passed on to senior government officials of Mexico their names," he said.
Gelbard said U.S. officials "have concerns about Governor Beltrones. And we're studying that. We're continuing to study that."
Mexican Attorney-General Jorge Madrazo Cuellar told reporters on Monday that Mexican authorities were not currently investigating either governor for any crime.

Beltrones governs the northwestern state of Sonora, through which large amounts of illegal drugs are smuggled on their way into the United States. He was considered one of the governors who was closest politically to disgraced former president Carlos Salinas.

Beltrones' six-year term ends in a few months and he cannot stand for re-election. Political analysts, however, say Beltrones has successfully chosen a candidate of his own for the July governor's election in Sonora. They suggest that some U.S. officials might be attempting to bring up the issue of his alleged drug ties in order to stop his preferred successor from winning.
